Asking politely, Italians say vorrei (I'd like): “Vorrei un caffè.”

rules.title: Il and la: every noun is masculine or feminine

body.text: Every Italian noun is masculine or feminine. “The” is il (masculine) or la (feminine); before a vowel both become l'.
Words in -o are usually masculine, in -a feminine, and in -e either: il cane (the dog), la notte (the night).

why.text: Italian kept Latin's habit of grouping nouns as masculine or feminine. The article (il, la, un, una) shows which group.

body.text: The verb ending says who is doing it, so io (I), lui (he) and lei (she) are usually left out: “Ho una sorella.”
È on its own means he is, she is or it is: “È mio fratello.” Family words drop the article: mio fratello, not il mio fratello.

why.text: The verb's ending already says who is doing it, so io or lui is only added for emphasis or contrast.

A few common ones can go before: una bella casa, un buon caffè.

why.text: In Italian the noun comes first and the description follows. The ending matches so it's clear which noun it describes.

why.text: Italian treats hunger, thirst and fear as things you have, a different picture of the same feeling.

rules.title: Su + il = sul: little words join up

body.text: In, su (on), di (of) and a (to) merge with the article: su + il = sul, in + la = nella, a + il = al.
“Il libro è sul tavolo”, “vado al parco”. They sound natural quickly.

why.text: Italian merges small words: su + il = sul, in + il = nel. It's faster to say, and it became the rule.

body.text: For tu, the command is often the same as “he does”: gira (turn), vai (go), prendi (take).
To a stranger, use the polite Lei form: giri a sinistra, vada dritto.

why.text: Commands use a short, direct form of the verb. The polite Lei form borrows from the subjunctive, which softens it.

rules.title: Lei: the polite “you”

body.text: With strangers, shop staff and older people, Italians use Lei, which takes the same verb as “she”: “Ha un'altra taglia?”
Tu is for friends, family and people your age who've said so.

rules.title: Mi alzo: verbs you do to yourself

body.text: Some verbs come with mi, ti or si when you do them to yourself: mi alzo (I get up), mi vesto (I get dressed).
The mi goes right before the verb: “Mi chiamo Anna” (I call myself Anna).

why.text: With these verbs you do the action to yourself, so mi, ti or si shows you're both the one acting and the one it happens to.

rules.title: The past: ho mangiato, sono andato

body.text: The everyday past uses avere or essere + participle: ho mangiato (I ate), ho visto (I saw).
Verbs of movement and change take essere, and the ending matches: sono andato (a man), sono andata (a woman).

why.text: Most verbs make the past with avere; verbs of movement and change (andare, venire…) use essere, a habit from Latin.

rules.title: Two past tenses: the scene and the event

body.text: The imperfect sets the scene or says what used to happen: abitava (she lived), andava (she would go).
Fairy tales tell the event with the passato remoto: trovò (she found). In speech you'd say “ha trovato”.

why.text: Italian uses the imperfetto for the background (what was going on) and the passato prossimo for events. Together they tell a story.

body.text: To say something had already happened, use the imperfect of avere or essere + participle: era andato via (had left), aveva mangiato (had eaten).
Mentre (while) + imperfect gives the background: “Mentre cucinavo, è squillato il telefono.”

why.text: Era or aveva plus a participle puts one past event before another, like English 'had done'.

rules.title: Ho mal di… and mi fa male

body.text: “Ho mal di testa” (I have a headache), “ho mal di gola” (sore throat), “ho mal di pancia” (stomachache).
Pointing: “Mi fa male qui” (it hurts me here). Da means “since”: “la febbre da ieri”.

why.text: Ho mal di… is literally 'I have pain of…', and mi fa male works like piacere: the thing that hurts is the subject.

rules.title: Giving advice: dovresti, se fossi in te, and the subjunctive

body.text: “Dovresti…” (you should…) is gentle advice. “Se fossi in te…” (if I were you…) uses the imperfect subjunctive.
After “è importante che”, the verb goes into the subjunctive: “che tu beva”. “Ti consiglio di” takes a plain verb.

why.text: Advice is about what hasn't happened yet, so Italian uses the conditional (dovresti) or the subjunctive.

rules.title: Tu or Lei?

body.text: Start with Lei with strangers, older people and at work. Friends, family and young people use tu.
“Possiamo darci del tu?” (can we use tu?) is the polite way to switch.

table: to use tu with each other

why.text: Tu is for friends and family; Lei for strangers, elders and work. The choice shows how close you are.

body.text: The conditional softens a request: potrebbe (could you), sarebbe (would it be), saprebbe (would you know).
“Mi saprebbe dire…?” (could you tell me…?) is a favorite polite opener.

why.text: Polite requests use the conditional and questions to give the other person room to say no.

rules.title: Idioms: learn them whole

body.text: An idiom means something different from its words. Avere la testa tra le nuvole, 'to have your head in the clouds', means to be daydreaming.
Learn each one as a block with a situation. Change only the verb for the person.

table: Mi è costato un occhio della testa.
It cost an arm and a leg.

why.text: Idioms are pictures a language has kept for centuries. Their meaning comes from the picture, not the single words.

rules.title: Telling a story: the linking words

body.text: Insomma, 'so, basically', brings in the point. Morale della favola, 'the moral of the fable', means 'long story short'.
E come se non bastasse, 'and as if that weren't enough', adds the last straw. Alla fine, 'in the end', wraps up.

why.text: These words tell the listener where the story is going, so it's easy to follow.
